extracted.intended_audience: Undergraduate students in CS103 (Discrete Structures) writing proofs
extracted.subtask_description: Checklist and stylistic rules for writing proofs about functions, graphs, and other discrete-structures topics, emphasizing correct use of first-order definitions, variable scope, and notation. Intended to be applied to homework proofs (starting with Problem Set Three) and used in grading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriately call back to first-order definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: When proofs involve definitions written in first-order logic, set up your assumptions and goals to match the structure of those definitions rather than writing unrelated or mismatched proof setups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify explicitly what you are assuming and what you must prove by translating the goal into the corresponding first-order structure. Do not pick arbitrary variables or start a proof whose structure corresponds to a different logical form than the target statement. Example anti-pattern: trying to prove ∀b ∃a f(a)=b (surjectivity) by first picking arbitrary x1,x2 ∈ A and assuming x1 ≠ x2 — that sets up a different quantifier pattern (∀x1 ∀x2 (x1≠x2 → …)). Be wary of high-level appeals (e.g., 'properties of f^3 transmit to f'); instead, prove each required component (injective and surjective) by appealing directly to the formal definitions. Use provided proof templates (Guide to Proofs on Discrete Structures) as starting points and check your proof setup before you begin writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don’t use quantifiers or connectives in your proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid using symbols like ∀, ∃, ∧, ∨, → in the prose of your written proofs; express quantification and logical structure in natural-language proof conventions instead.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a conventional style enforced in the course (not a logical necessity). Replace formal quantifier notation with standard phrasing such as 'consider an arbitrary b ∈ B' instead of 'consider ∀b ∈ B'. Example anti-pattern: restating the formal definition inside the proof as 'we need to prove that ∀b ∈ B. ∃a ∈ A. f(a)=b' — instead state 'consider an arbitrary b ∈ B; we need to show there exists a ∈ A with f(a)=b.' If unsure about a construction that seems to demand first-order notation, consult instructors or office hours for advice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don’t repeat definitions; use them instead
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not restate definitions in the abstract; apply them directly to the specific variables or objects in your proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assume the reader knows the definitions and show how those definitions apply to the particular elements or cases under consideration. Repeating definitions verbatim is redundant, often introduces scoping errors, and lengthens proofs. Example anti-patterns: sentences like 'every element of A is an element of B' or 'every x ∈ A satisfies x ∈ B' can be ambiguous or create variable-scope mistakes. Preferred concise form: 'Since x ∈ A and A ⊆ B, we see that x ∈ B.' Example with involution: instead of writing 'for any a1 ∈ A, f(f(a1)) = a1' after already picking a specific a1, simply write 'we know f is an involution, so f(f(a1)) = a1.' This avoids accidentally switching between 'for all' and 'for this specific' and keeps variable roles clear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish between assuming and proving
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat assumed statements and statements you must prove differently: assuming a statement can give you new introduced variables (or let you apply its consequences), while proving a statement requires constructing witnesses or working from arbitrary choices per the quantifier structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand how existential vs universal structure affects your proof strategy. Example: 'n is even' (∃k n=2k) — to prove n is even you must find a k; to assume n is even you can introduce a k with n=2k. For injectivity (a universal statement), when proving injective you should pick arbitrary x1,x2 ∈ A and assume f(x1)=f(x2) to show x1=x2; when assuming injectivity you do not introduce new variables but wait for particular y1,y2 with f(y1)=f(y2) to conclude y1=y2. Anti-pattern: introducing variables when you only have a universally-quantified assumption (e.g., saying 'for any x1 ∈ A, f(f(x1)) = x1' after merely assuming involution) — that mixes scopes and typically breaks the proof. Heuristics to detect mixing up: sentences that say 'for all x' in a place where you are only assuming something, or starting with arbitrary choices and later discovering you needed a specific value. If confused, delete the suspect paragraph and re-start the setup correctly, or ask instructors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Type-check your proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure that expressions and statements respect the types of the objects involved (e.g., distinguish between functions and elements: f is a function, f(x) is an element of the codomain).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid category mistakes like asserting properties that apply to functions about specific function values (e.g., do not write 'f(x) is injective' or 'f(x) is a bijection' since f(x) is an element, not a function). Keep notation distinct to show understanding of what each symbol denotes. Note: mathematicians sometimes loosen this distinction in informal writing, but for the purposes of the course you should be strict to convince graders you understand the concepts.
